cells.tense: You are holding what you know until the moment is actually right for it.
cells.ask: Tell one person the thing you have been holding, somewhere it can be heard and nothing hangs on it landing well.
cells.core:
You hold what you know until the moment is right. Not hesitating — weighing. Two readings sit side by side and you wait for the one that will still be true when you say it out loud.

That waiting is the useful part, and it does something here. Around anything young, rushing an answer flattens it. You let the answer arrive on its own and then you know. What keeps this working is knowing when the waiting has gone on too long. You can offer a piece before it's finished: one plain sentence about what you see coming, to the person tending it with you, then let them say what they think.

cells.tense: You are reaching for a certainty that has not arrived yet, and you are reaching early.
cells.ask: Leave one question unanswered for a week, and when you come back, write down only what the week showed you.
cells.core:
You want to know ahead of time how this turns out. So you run the answers forward, testing each one against a future you can't see — what they'll say, how it lands, what to do if it doesn't. The weighing doesn't stop when the information does.

What gets lost is the thing itself. Tending works on its own schedule, and your bracing keeps pulling it toward a day that hasn't come. Coming back to the present sometimes means letting one question stay open on purpose, past the point where you would normally settle it. What you're waiting for is a knowing that arrives without you forcing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're running the answers ahead of the thing itself.

cells.tense: You read what's happening with what you tend, and it stays inside you.
cells.ask: Do one unfinished thing this week in front of someone you trust, before it's any good.
cells.core:
You see what's happening with what you tend — what it needs, what it isn't ready for — and little of it comes out of your mouth. Someone else says it, or it goes unsaid and you wait. The attention is all there. The saying isn't.

A young thing can take your read even when it's rough. What it can't take is nothing, and nothing is what quiet hands it. Today that's small and public: put one unfinished thing in front of a person who won't grade it, say the plain thing you notice, and let their face tell you what lands.

cells.tense: You are already sorting what's worth saying, and you call it just following the thing along.
cells.ask: Name one call you made about what this is becoming, out loud, and put your name on it.
cells.core:
You're already reading what this needs and holding back what isn't ripe. It shows in what you don't say yet, what you water, what you let sit. Read well, that judgment is steady and accurate — you know what's next because you were paying attention, and the thing grows on a schedule you helped set. You just don't say you set it.

So it reads as luck, or as the thing doing it on its own. A judgment you keep to yourself can't be checked later or corrected out loud. Try owning one plainly: this is what's happening here — and then let them answer.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading this. Say so.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that a finished inner knowing is already being withheld on purpose in the Balanced cell — the record gives the mechanism, not the person's history, so the core describes the holding and lets them disown it. The reader could reasonably say the sorting is ordinary caution or other people's opinions in their head, and the asks survive that: each one is an act they can do today whether or not my read is right.
